explanations.explanation: That's the word David uses. He tells the assembly that Solomon, his son and the king God chose, is “…young and inexperienced.” I think that's a dad being honest, not harsh. Nobody is born knowing how to build a temple, and I couldn't stamp a straight line my first day either.

David never calls Solomon rebellious. He says Solomon, the one God has chosen, is “…young and inexperienced.” Those are two very different problems, friend. Inexperienced just means he hasn't done it yet, and that gets better with time.

David doesn't say a word about Solomon being unwilling. What he says is that Solomon is “…young and inexperienced.” Being new at a job isn't the same as not wanting it. Plenty of us have wanted a job long before we were any good at it.

explanations.answer: The palace is for the LORD God
explanations.explanation: David gives the reason right away: “The task is great because this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.” The size of the job comes from who it's for. Building for a neighbor is one thing. Building for the LORD God is another level entirely.

explanations.answer: The land is full of enemies
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention enemies here. He says the task is great because “…this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.” The weight of the job comes from who it's for. It has nothing to do with who's outside the walls.

David doesn't say anything about the number of workers. His reason is that “…this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God.” So the job is great because of who it's for, not because of the headcount. Even a huge crew would still be building for the LORD God.
David says he gives “…my personal treasures of gold and silver…” That's over and above all that he had provided for the temple. These are his own treasures, and he's the one giving them.

David says nothing about borrowing. He says he gives “…my personal treasures of gold and silver…” Those are his own, over and above all that he had already provided. Giving your own is a lot different than passing along somebody else's.

The text doesn't say these treasures were captured. David calls them “…my personal treasures of gold and silver…” They belong to him, and he's giving them over and above everything else he had provided. That's a gift from his own pocket.

explanations.answer: His delight in the house of his God
explanations.explanation: David gives his reason himself: “Moreover, because of my delight in the house of my God, I now give for it my personal treasures of gold and silver…” He gives because he delights in the house of his God. When you love something, giving to it feels more like joy than a bill.

explanations.answer: Nathan the prophet told him to
explanations.explanation: Nathan is the prophet named at the end of this chapter, but this passage doesn't say he told David to give. David gives the reason himself: “…because of my delight in the house of my God…” So the gift comes from what David loves. I'd leave Nathan out of this one.

This passage doesn't mention the leaders asking David for anything. David names his own reason: “…because of my delight in the house of my God…” He gives first, and then he asks the assembly a question. The reason he names is delight.

explanations.answer: Who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today
explanations.explanation: David asks, “Now who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” He doesn't order anyone. He asks who is willing. After giving his own gold and silver, he opens the door for everyone else.

explanations.answer: Who will march out against the Philistines with me
explanations.explanation: This passage has no march against the Philistines. David's question is, “Now who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” It's a question about being willing to consecrate yourself to the LORD.

explanations.answer: Who will go up to Lebanon to cut cedar
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask anyone to go to Lebanon in this passage. He asks, “Now who is willing to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” That's a question about willing hearts, not a trip with an axe. Nobody needs hiking boots for this one.

The text says the opposite. The leaders “gave willingly” (1 Chronicles 29:6), and David asked who was willing, not who was ordered. Even the people rejoiced because the leaders had given “…freely and wholeheartedly.” (1 Chronicles 29:9). You can't order that kind of joy, friend.

That's right. The leaders “gave willingly” (1 Chronicles 29:6), and the text says it plainly. David asked who was willing, and they stepped up. The people rejoiced because the leaders had given “…freely and wholeheartedly.” (1 Chronicles 29:9).

The text says, “…the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders…” They had given to the LORD “…freely and wholeheartedly.” and King David also rejoiced greatly. When giving comes from the heart, the whole room feels it. I can hop on my gold base just reading it.

There's no grumbling in this passage. The people “…rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders…” The leaders gave “…freely and wholeheartedly.” and that made the room glad. King David also rejoiced greatly.

Nobody argues here. The text says “…the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders…” The gifts were given “…freely and wholeheartedly.” and King David also rejoiced greatly. That's a whole assembly pulling the same direction.

explanations.answer: Everything in heaven and on earth is His
explanations.explanation: David says it right in his prayer: “…for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You.” That's why the greatness, the power and the glory are the LORD's. When everything is already His, there's nothing left to compete with Him.

explanations.answer: He won every battle for Israel
explanations.explanation: David doesn't give battles as the reason here. He says the greatness, the power and the glory are the LORD's “…for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You.” His reason is bigger than any one fight. It covers heaven and earth.

explanations.answer: His temple will be the greatest one
explanations.explanation: David doesn't point to the temple as his reason. He says it's “…for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You.” The temple is a gift to the LORD, and it doesn't make Him great. The LORD already owns everything, with or without a building.

David prays, “Both riches and honor come from You, and You are the ruler over all.” He's talking to the LORD, so the answer is right there in his prayer. Think about that: this man had just handed over a mountain of gold, and he still says it all comes from God.
David is the king, and he still doesn't claim it. He prays to the LORD, “Both riches and honor come from You…” A king with all that gold knows where it came from, and that humbles me every time.

David doesn't say hard work in this prayer. He says to the LORD, “Both riches and honor come from You…” Work is real, but David points past it to the One who gives. Some folks give themselves a whole lot of credit, and David isn't one of them.

explanations.answer: Everything comes from God's own hand
explanations.explanation: David answers his own question this way: “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.” They gave generously, but what they gave came from God's own hand. That's the whole secret.

explanations.answer: The people worked extra hard all year
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say anything about the people working extra hard. His answer is, “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.” He gives the credit to God, not to the effort. I wouldn't have thought to pray that, but David did.

explanations.answer: The king of Tyre sent them help
explanations.explanation: The king of Tyre doesn't come up in this prayer at all. David's answer is, “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.” He doesn't point to a helper. He points to God's own hand.

David prays, “I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness.” God looks at the heart, not just what we hand over. That's why David talks about giving willingly and with an upright heart.

David doesn't say hands. He says to God, “I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness.” The hands did the giving, but the heart is what God tests. You can fill your hands with gold and still miss it, friend.

David doesn't say tongue here. He says, “I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness.” Fancy words are easy, and a heart is a lot harder to fake. God tests the part that talk can't cover.

David says the opposite. He tells God, “All these things I have given willingly and with an upright heart…” Nothing grudging about it. He also says he's seen the people giving “…joyfully and willingly…”

That's right. David tells God, “All these things I have given willingly and with an upright heart…” He also says he saw the people there giving “…joyfully and willingly to You.” No grudge anywhere in that prayer.

explanations.answer: The same desire they just showed
explanations.explanation: David asks, “O LORD, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, keep this desire forever in the intentions of the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You.” The desire is the willing giving they had just shown. David wants it to last, and he asks God to point their hearts toward Him.

David doesn't ask for fear of enemies. He asks God to “…keep this desire forever in the intentions of the hearts of Your people…” The desire he means is the willing giving they just showed. He also asks God to direct their hearts toward Him.

David doesn't pray for pride in the temple. He asks God to “…keep this desire forever in the intentions of the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You.” His focus is on hearts turned toward God. That's a lot better than hearts turned toward a building.

David prays for Solomon, “…a whole heart to keep and carry out all Your commandments, decrees, and statutes, and to build Your palace for which I have made provision.” Building is the job David is praying about. David has made provision, and now he prays for Solomon's heart. A good dad does both.

David doesn't say guard. He asks for Solomon “…a whole heart to keep and carry out all Your commandments, decrees, and statutes, and to build Your palace for which I have made provision.” The job in the prayer is building. David already did the stockpiling.

David doesn't say inherit. His prayer is that Solomon would have a whole heart “…to keep and carry out all Your commandments, decrees, and statutes, and to build Your palace…” The word in the prayer is build. David made provision, and now he prays for Solomon to build.

That's what the text says: “They bowed down and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.” The whole assembly blessed the LORD first, since David had told them to. Then they bowed to the LORD and to the king.

Good thinking, but this one is true, friend. After the whole assembly blessed the LORD, “They bowed down and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.” The text puts both in the same line, the LORD and the king.

The text says, “Then, for a second time, they designated David’s son Solomon as king, anointing him before the LORD as ruler…” Solomon is David's son, and he's now the king. A second time means he'd been made king before, and this time it's out in the open with the whole assembly.

There's no battle here. The text says they designated Solomon, David's son, as king for a second time, “…anointing him before the LORD as ruler…” It's a crowning day, not a war day. He gets a throne, not a sword.
The text names Zadok as the priest. Solomon, David's son, is anointed “as ruler.” That's a king's job, not a priest's. Two anointings, two different jobs.
The text says they anointed Solomon “…as ruler, and Zadok as the priest.” Solomon is anointed as ruler, and Zadok is anointed as the priest. Two jobs, two people, one big day.

Abiathar isn't the name this verse gives. It says Solomon was anointed “…as ruler, and Zadok as the priest.” So the priest in this verse is Zadok. Names are easy to mix up, friend, and I've called a rolling pin a spatula before.

Eli is a priest from the earlier stories, at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9), but he isn't the one here. This verse says Solomon was anointed “…as ruler, and Zadok as the priest.” So the name to remember is Zadok. Eli belongs to a different chapter of Israel's story.

explanations.answer: He prospers and all Israel obeys him
explanations.explanation: The text says, “So Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of his father David. He prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.” The reign begins with success and a whole nation behind him. It's a strong start for a king who was called young and inexperienced.
Nothing like that happens here. The text says Solomon “…prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.” Israel is together under him at the start of his reign. This chapter only shows that beginning.

explanations.answer: The tribes rise up against him
explanations.explanation: This passage doesn't mention a rising up. It says Solomon “…prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.” Obedience from all Israel is what the text records for his reign here.

That's what the text says: “All the officials and mighty men, as well as all of King David’s sons, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.” Even David's own sons were in on it. Nobody was left out of that line.

Here's the surprise: it's true, friend. “All the officials and mighty men, as well as all of King David’s sons, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.” Even David's own sons are in that line. Nobody was left out of it.

The text says something different. The LORD “…bestowed on him royal majesty such as had not been bestowed on any king in Israel before him.” So it wasn't the same as the earlier kings had. No king in Israel before him had been given royal majesty like that.

That's right. The LORD “…bestowed on him royal majesty such as had not been bestowed on any king in Israel before him.” It wasn't the same. Not a single king in Israel before him had been given what Solomon was given.
The text says David's reign was “…seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” That adds up to forty years, and I checked it twice with my mustache. Hebron came first, then Jerusalem.

Bethlehem isn't the place this verse names. It says David reigned “…seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” So Hebron is the place for the seven years. Together with the thirty-three in Jerusalem, that makes the forty.
Shiloh isn't named in this verse. It says David reigned “…seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.” Hebron holds the first seven years. Jerusalem holds the rest.

explanations.answer: He dies at a ripe old age full of honor
explanations.explanation: The text says, “He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor, and his son Solomon reigned in his place.” It's a full life with a full finish. Years, riches and honor are the three things the text says he was full of.

explanations.answer: He falls in battle against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That isn't how the text ends David's life. It says, “He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor…” No battlefield in that verse. His son Solomon reigned in his place.

explanations.answer: He dies alone and forgotten in the palace
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't describe that. It says David “…died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor…” and his acts are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the Seer, Nathan the Prophet and Gad the Seer. That's a life people wrote down, friend.
